opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's something we think about a lot, because the autoregressive world has had years of incredibly hard engineering and research go into it. There's a whole playbook now: large-scale pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, instruction tuning, preference optimization, RLHF, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, distillation, and so on. One of the things we've found is that a surprising amount of that playbook carries over to diffusion language models, but not always in a plug-and-play way.

At a high level, the data and the overall pipeline look very similar. You still pretrain on a large corpus of text and code, you still do a fine-tuning phase to get the model to follow instructions, and you still want some kind of alignment or RL stage at the end. What changes is the objective at each stage. In an autoregressive model, everything is built around next-token prediction, so you have a clean, exact log-likelihood that factorizes left to right. Many techniques quietly rely on that. With a diffusion model, you're training the network to denoise, to take a corrupted sequence, say with some tokens masked out, and predict what the clean tokens should be. You don't get an exact likelihood for free; you get a bound on it, something like an evidence lower bound. So whenever a technique depends on computing the probability of a sequence exactly, you have to stop and ask how to adapt it.

Supervised fine-tuning is the easy case. You condition on the prompt and apply the denoising objective only to the response tokens. That works very naturally, and in some ways diffusion is even more flexible there, because you aren't locked into left-to-right generation. You can do infilling, editing, or condition on pieces at the end of the sequence just as easily as at the beginning.

Preference optimization and RL are more interesting. Methods like DPO or policy-gradient approaches such as PPO or GRPO are written in terms of log-probabilities of the generated output under the policy. For a diffusion model you have to substitute something, often the ELBO or some estimate of it, and then think carefully about the variance of that estimate and whether the gradients you get actually point in the right direction. There's been nice work in the community, and some of our own, showing that if you do this carefully you can get the same kinds of gains from alignment and from RL on reasoning tasks that people see with autoregressive models.

There's also the inference side, which feeds back into training. Diffusion models generate by iteratively refining the whole sequence in parallel over a number of denoising steps, and that's where the big speed advantage comes from, since you're not paying one forward pass per token. So you want to train in a way that makes the model good at producing high-quality outputs in a small number of steps. That's where ideas like distillation and consistency-style training, which came from the image diffusion world, become really important. In a sense we get to borrow from two toolboxes: the language-model toolbox for data, scaling, and alignment, and the diffusion toolbox for fast sampling and controllability.

So the way I'd summarize it: the high-level recipe transfers remarkably well, but the details matter. Wherever a method assumes autoregressive factorization, you have to rethink it in terms of the denoising objective. And when you do that carefully, you often find extra flexibility you didn't have before.

r001.rationale: It identifies denoising instead of next-token prediction as the objective for pretraining and fine-tuning, but does not identify mid-training.

r002.rationale: It explains that RL methods relying on output log-probabilities need adaptation for diffusion models, using an ELBO or estimate and accounting for its variance and gradient direction.

r003.rationale: It discusses denoising steps and inference speed, but does not identify generating rollouts as the dominant computational cost of RL post-training.

r004.rationale: It connects diffusion sampling speed to distillation and consistency training, but not to expanded possibilities for RL post-training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the things I find most exciting about the whole direction, because when we started working on diffusion language models, there was this worry that we'd have to throw away everything the field had learned about training autoregressive models and start from scratch. And it turns out that's mostly not true. A lot of the infrastructure, the data pipelines, the tokenizers, the architectures, the optimizer recipes, all of that carries over almost directly. The transformer is still a transformer. What changes is the training objective and the way you generate.

So the way I think about it is, there are really three layers. The first is pretraining, and here the core difference is that instead of predicting the next token given the prefix, you're corrupting the sequence, masking out some fraction of the tokens, and training the model to recover them. That's a different loss, but it's still a maximum-likelihood style objective, and you can derive a proper variational bound on the log-likelihood, which was something that took the community a while to get right. Once you have that, scaling laws, learning rate schedules, batch sizes, a lot of the empirical knowledge transfers surprisingly well. We've even found you can take an existing autoregressive checkpoint and adapt it into a diffusion model with a relatively small amount of additional compute, rather than training from zero. That's a huge practical win.

The second layer is post-training, so instruction tuning and alignment. Supervised fine-tuning is almost trivially the same, you just apply the masked denoising loss on the response tokens conditioned on the prompt. Where it gets more interesting is RL and preference optimization. Methods like PPO or DPO are built around the idea that you can compute the log-probability of a sampled sequence under the policy, and in an autoregressive model that's exact and cheap. In a diffusion model you only have a bound on the likelihood, and it's expensive to evaluate. So you have to be a bit clever, either using the ELBO as a surrogate, or designing reward-weighted objectives that work directly on the denoising steps. There's been a lot of nice work on this recently and I think it's largely a solved problem now, but it's a place where you can't just copy and paste.

And the third layer is inference, which is really where diffusion models shine, because you get to decouple the training recipe from the generation strategy. You can trade off quality and speed by choosing how many denoising steps to run, you can generate tokens in parallel, you can do infilling and editing natively, and you can use things like confidence-based unmasking or remasking to improve quality. Techniques like speculative decoding or KV caching, which were designed for sequential generation, need to be rethought, but there are natural analogs.

So my overall view is, don't think of it as a different field. Think of it as the same field with one dial changed, which is how you factorize the joint distribution over tokens. Most of the engineering wisdom transfers, a few pieces need real rethinking, and those few pieces are exactly where the interesting research is right now.

r001.rationale: It describes denoising for pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, but does not identify mid-training as requiring that adaptation.

r002.rationale: It explains that diffusion models lack cheap exact sequence log-probabilities and describes using ELBO surrogates or reward-weighted denoising-step objectives for RL.

r003.rationale: It mentions costly likelihood evaluation, but does not identify generating rollouts as the dominant RL post-training cost.

r004.rationale: It discusses faster, parallel inference and RL post-training separately, without connecting faster inference to expanded RL possibilities.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot we can reuse, but we have to be careful about what depends on the autoregressive formulation. At a high level, you still have pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and potentially reinforcement learning or preference optimization. Those ideas are not specific to predicting the next token.

But the actual training objectives can be quite different. With a diffusion language model, you’re learning to recover text from a corrupted version of it, so even in supervised fine-tuning, you have choices about how much to corrupt the response and what to keep fixed as context.

Preference optimization is another interesting example. Many existing methods use the probability of a response, which is straightforward to compute for an autoregressive model. For diffusion models, that computation is generally more challenging. So you need to think about what quantity you can estimate and whether it gives you the learning signal you want.

So my view is: transfer the principles, but revisit the assumptions. We shouldn’t assume that the exact recipe developed for autoregressive models is also the best recipe for diffusion.

r001.rationale: The response describes diffusion training as recovering text from corrupted text and discusses SFT choices, but does not identify replacing next-token prediction as the central adaptation across pretraining, mid-training, and SFT.

r002.rationale: It says response probabilities are harder to compute for diffusion models, but does not explain how their sampling process changes the propagation of reinforcement-learning reward information.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify rollout generation as the dominant computational cost of RL post-training.

r004.rationale: The response does not connect faster diffusion-model inference to expanded RL post-training possibilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot we can borrow, but we have to be careful about which parts depend on the autoregressive formulation. With an autoregressive model, you have this very natural decomposition into next-token prediction. With a diffusion model, you’re learning to denoise, potentially making predictions about many tokens at once, and conditioning on different amounts of corrupted information.

So something like supervised fine-tuning is fairly natural: you can take examples of the behavior you want and adapt the denoising objective. But when you move to preference optimization or reinforcement learning, some of the machinery needs to change. A lot of existing methods assume that you can easily compute the probability of a response as a product of token probabilities. That’s less straightforward with diffusion.

The way I would approach it is to preserve the goal of those techniques—learning from demonstrations, preferences, or rewards—but derive the objective for the diffusion process itself. And then there’s an opportunity to exploit what’s different about diffusion, like being able to revise multiple parts of an answer together, rather than just trying to reproduce the autoregressive pipeline.

r001.rationale: It contrasts next-token prediction with denoising and says SFT can adapt the denoising objective, but does not identify this as the adaptation for pre-training, mid-training, and SFT.

r002.rationale: It says preference optimization and RL machinery may need to change, but does not explain how the sampling process changes reward propagation back into the network.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify rollout generation as the dominant computational cost of RL post-training.

r004.rationale: It mentions revising multiple parts of an answer together, but does not connect faster diffusion inference to expanded RL post-training possibilities.
